units.text: We'll walk through what makes a secure agent decision observable. Retrieved material can help answer the user's question, but it cannot authorize an export or any separate action. The application retains that decision.
When an out-of-scope action is proposed, the policy and application validation deny it. Confirm no tool call ran and no data moved. Record the reason and return only the authorized answer.
For the fictional refund, the reviewer must see the order, amount, account and reason. The workflow waits for that decision. A rejection or timeout ends without issuing a refund.

If the request is approved, recheck the current order and approved scope. Execute only the approved refund and record what the service returned. If the amount changes or the order is no longer eligible, don't rely on the old approval.

Start with the caller, then check the proposed tool and parameters, the gateway decision, and finally the target's own permission. Use correlation identifiers to connect the evidence instead of broadening permissions before you know which layer denied it.
Repair only an unintended denial. Then test one authorized request that should succeed and an unauthorized one that should still fail. A denied request can be exactly the expected secure result.

We'll follow a versioned template into a managed stack. The template records desired resources and their relationships so the same design can be reviewed and repeated. CloudFormation uses it to create or update the stack in its target account and Region.

CloudFormation compares the proposed template with the managed stack and produces a change set. Look for what will be added, removed, or potentially replaced, especially data-bearing resources. A preview is not yet a change.
Execute only an approved change set, then read the stack events. The preview cannot guarantee success or expose every property-level effect. Verify the resources and workload after the operation.

When CloudFormation deletes the stack or removes a resource from its template, DeletionPolicy governs what happens for that resource. Delete removes it, Retain leaves it outside stack management, and Snapshot takes a backup before removing certain supported resources.

Don't assume retention is free or that Snapshot works for every type. Verify the resource-specific defaults and prerequisites. When an update replaces the physical resource, check UpdateReplacePolicy instead.

A property change can require a new physical database. UpdateReplacePolicy applies to the old database during that replacement. If the old data needs to survive, choose the appropriate supported policy and validate recovery in advance.

If the new database later leaves the stack, its DeletionPolicy applies. Those are two different moments. Test the restored data and new connection details rather than assuming the old endpoint follows the resource.

We'll extend a stack when a native resource doesn't cover the required action. CloudFormation sends the configured provider a create, update, or delete request, then waits for the provider response. The response determines whether that lifecycle step can continue.

Keep the physical resource identifier stable for an in-place update. Handle retries and deletes safely so the same lifecycle event doesn't produce extra side effects. A missing response may eventually fail the stack operation.

A StackSet coordinates deployments from one template across selected accounts and Regions. The diagram shows why each combination needs separate verification: an instance can be recorded for a target even if the stack there failed.

Choose self-managed permissions when you manage the required roles. For supported organization-based deployments, service-managed permissions use Organizations trusted access. Inspect operation and target results instead of treating a submitted job as fleet-wide success.

With service-managed StackSets and auto deployment, an eligible account entering the target organizational unit can receive the stack. New accounts use the StackSet default parameters; an override on an existing account isn't automatically inherited.

When an account leaves, stack removal or retention follows the configured option. Check the affected stack instance and underlying operation status. Auto deployment is not automatic repair for unrelated stack failures.

We'll reconcile an out-of-band change without blindly undoing it. A drift-aware change set compares the previous deployment, actual live state and desired template for supported resources. Here the live versioning setting differs from the last deployment.

If the live setting is approved, update the desired template to match. If it isn't intended, review the proposed revert before execution. Check supported resources and properties and verify the resulting live state.

The template references Secrets Manager rather than storing the secret value. CloudFormation resolves it when creating or updating the resource that uses it. Scope access and avoid exposing the resolved secret in application logs.

A secret changing does not trigger CloudFormation to read it again automatically. Rotation and runtime consumption have their own workflow. Verify that the intended consumer refreshes its credentials rather than assuming a new secret value updated every resource.

Use a supported physical identifier and a template describing the stack. Include the required DeletionPolicy and review the import change set. The operation should adopt the bucket, not create a new one or change unrelated resources.

After import, check that the original bucket and data are present and run supported drift detection. Import changes management ownership; it does not guarantee every property matches the declared template.

Automatic import needs a supported resource with the required static name and retention policy, and the resource must not already belong to a stack. Enable the intended import option and inspect the proposed operation.
Use manual import when the resource type is eligible but you need to supply its physical identifier. Neither mode works for every resource. Check ownership and detect any drift after adoption.

We'll follow an approved product through Service Catalog. The administrator publishes the version into a portfolio. An authorized user selects and launches it. With a launch constraint, the provisioning role is separate from the user's own identity.
Allow the right audience to launch the product and constrain the allowed parameter values where supported. If the request doesn't meet those conditions, reject it before provisioning anything.

An approved launch uses the configured role. That constraint selects the role, but it doesn't make the role's underlying policy narrower. Scope permission to the required actions and resources, then verify the product behaves as intended.
